newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea moves closer to first hostile takeover.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea moves closer to first hostile takeover.

text.p: South Korea moved closer to its first-ever hostile takeover on Thursday after a Seoul-based hotel made a tender offer to secure an absolute majority stake in garment maker New Star Trading Co
The Savoy Hotel, located in the capital's major shopping district of Myongdong, offered to buy a further 25.3 percent of New Star's shares from May 6 to May 25 at 62,500 won ($70) each.

If successful, Savoy's stake in New Star would rise to 50 percent from 24.7 percent currently, according to Securities Supervisory Board data. New Korean rules give an absolute majority stake to anyone who accumulates 50 percent of a company's shares plus one.

News of the tender offer sent New Star shares plunging to their daily limit as investors viewed the takeover attempt as almost concluded, analysts said. New Star closed Thursday's trading down 4,900 won at 57,200 won.

"Many people think the game is finished as they see few choices left for New Star to defend itself," said analyst Kim Ik-hwan of Hyundai Securities. "This is also a 'buy on rumours, sell on news' trading pattern."
Adding to the speculation, New Star's management gave no immediate response and a company executive said it was undecided about how to counter Savoy's tender offer.
"We have not yet decided on how to ward off the attack," New Star's executive director Kim Hong-gil told Reuters. "But it does not mean we are surrendering."
New Star is currently held by the family of its president, Kim Hong-kun, who had a combined stake of 29.26 percent as of April 15, according to Securities Supervisory Board data.

Last Friday, Kim said the company was safe from any hostile takeover bid and would make every effort to defend itself. He issued a plea for a white knight, but no one has officially attempted a rescue.
He also said he was considering a separate tender offer.
Also on Friday, New Star said it would buy back five percent of its shares from April 21-July 20.
Two days earlier it announced a plan to offer a one-for-100 bonus issue on May 2 to raise the existing owner's stake and to seek a chance to analyse New Star's shareholding structure.
Hostile takeovers were nearly impossible in South Korea before new rules allowing share purchases of up to 25 percent of a firm without prior approval.
But the new regulations, which went into force on April 1, mandate that those who want to accumulate shares in excess of 25 percent make a tender offer.
Analysts said they expected more companies controlled by owners of relatively small stakes to come under attack from corporate raiders in the future.

"This case showed well how the new rules work. I expect similar cases to follow suit," said Park Byung-moon, head of research at LG Securities. "Existing owners will have to raise their ownership to prevent takeover attacks."

But a recent bid by edible oil maker Shindongbang Corp to take over Midopa Department Store Co fizzled out under pressure from a body representing the nation's leading conglomerates, known as Chaebol.
The Federation of Korean Industries openly opposed the takeover bid and pledged a joint action to help Midopa's owner, the Dainong Group, maintain its ownership.
